title: Quality Control Screening of Brain Organoid Morphology
author: Chiaradia, Boulanger, et al.

steps.title: Select day‑18 organoids
steps.instruction: Use neural organoids at day 18 and acquire brightfield images saved as TIFF files with a valid pixel calibration in microns.

steps.title: Open Fiji (ImageJ)
steps.instruction: Install the latest version of Fiji (ImageJ) and launch it (≈ 3 min).

steps.title: Load macro script
steps.instruction: In Fiji, open Plugins → New → Macro, copy‑paste the script from https://github.com/jboulanger/Organoid_morphology (Organoid_Morphology.ijm) into the editor and set the language to IJ1Macro.

steps.title: Run macro on images
steps.instruction: Press Run for a single image or Batch for multiple images, then choose an output folder where the result files will be saved.

steps.title: Verify input file format
steps.instruction: Make sure each input file is a TIFF with a valid pixel calibration in microns before running the macro.

steps.title: Choose segmentation mode
steps.instruction: Select manual segmentation if preferred (recommended for beta‑testing) or let the macro attempt automated segmentation.

substeps.instruction: For manual segmentation, use the polygon tool to trace the organoid contour and close the selection.
Save the ROI as filename.roi (≈ 2 KB).

steps.title: Handle automated segmentation errors
steps.instruction: Automated segmentation error ranges from 4.88 % (good) to 19.64 % (poor); manually re‑segment any poorly segmented samples.

steps.title: Set display options
steps.instruction: Choose overlay measures (e.g., DNE, curvature), enable Display Info, add a colorbar, set colorbar min/max values, and define marker scale for inflection points.

steps.title: Save annotated image
steps.instruction: Save the annotated image as a JPEG (hundreds of KB) and close the window.

steps.title: Batch processing of many images
steps.instruction: Run the macro in Batch mode to generate .jpg and .roi files for all images in the set.

steps.title: Inspect and correct segmentations
steps.instruction: Open each .jpg output, identify poorly segmented samples, manually re‑segment them, then re‑run the macro with ‘Use Saved ROI’ enabled for those files.

steps.title: Export results table
steps.instruction: After processing, save the compiled results as a .csv output table.

description: Organoids vary in form and fate, and there is no perfect protocol for every scientific question. Neural organoids can refer to guided (or patterned) and unguided (or unpatterned) protocols.2 Guided organoids display a more consistent shape and forebrain identity, whereas unguided organoids exhibit greater batch-to-batch and intra-batch variability but display the coexistence of different brain regional identities and increased tissue structure complexity.1,3 Unguided organoids include cerebral organoids or brain organoids,4,5 where neural differentiation from the pluripotent embryoid body (EB) is obtained by default and the presence of intrinsic brain signalling centres – cortical hem, pallium-subpallium boundary – confers self-patterning features.6 Conversly, in guided, patterned, or regionalised neural organoids the intrinsic signalling is overruled by exogenous patterning with added growth factor inhibitors, to obtain more homogenous tissue identity. Forebrain identity is induced through the combined inhibition of both TFGß and BMP pathways in cortical spheroids (CSs)7 and forebrain organoids.8 Cortical organoids9 are obtained through TFGß, BMP, and WNT inhibition. Serum-free floating culture of embryoid body-like aggregates with quick reaggregation (SFEBq) are instead obtained with concomitant TFGß and WNT inhibition.10 Ventral forebrain organoids,11 region-specific choroid plexus organoids,12,13 hippocampal organoids,12 cerebellar organoids,14,15,16 and retinal organoids17,18 are other examples of central nervous system (CNS) guided organoids obtained by similarly inhibiting or activating relevant patterning pathways, and displaying varying morphologies. Previous works have focused on achieving reproducibility in size of organoids,3,8 but morphology has remained largely overlooked and no guidelines have been drawn so far for the morphological parameters to be expected in neural organoids.
